paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35), or TYK2 deficiency, is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency. Its core feature is susceptibility to mycobacterial infections (including BCG disease and tuberculosis), viral infections, or both. Infections with other intracellular bacteria, such as Salmonella and Brucella, also occur. TYK2 deficiency was first described in a patient with features of hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES), including atopic dermatitis and elevated serum IgE. Most later-reported patients have not had HIES features, and serum IgE elevation varies (Kreins et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2020; Lv et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, born in 1992, who was the third child of healthy first-cousin parents. He was vaccinated with BCG at 2 months of age. At 8 months, left axillary lymphadenopathy was detected and isoniazid treatment was started. His course included disseminated BCG infection with generalized fistulous lymphadenopathy, fever, fatigue, and a negative PPD skin test. He later had pneumonia and herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve. He also had neurobrucellosis, with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, severe sensorineural hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, aggressive behavior, and lacunar infarcts in the temporal, occipital, and parietal lobes. Serum IgG, IgM, and IgA were normal, and serum IgE was mildly elevated. His antibody response to tetanus toxoid was low. His medical history included no atopy, asthma, or skin problems such as candidiasis, boils, folliculitis, or cold abscesses. He had no staphylococcal skin or lung infections and no skeletal or dental features of HIES. Kilic et al. (2012) noted that, unlike the Japanese TYK2-deficient patient, their patient lacked the cardinal features of HIES.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) restudied the Japanese patient (P1) originally reported by Minegishi et al. (2006). P1 was a man born to consanguineous parents. He had atopic dermatitis from 1 month of age and recurrent bacterial and viral infections from 1 year of age. His infections included BCGitis, nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis with sepsis, parainfluenza virus 3 pneumonia, recurrent oral herpes simplex virus infections, molluscum contagiosum, mild oral candidiasis, pneumonia without pneumatocele, otitis, and sinusitis. He also had recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses and ocular sarcoidosis. Repeated immunologic studies showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and high serum IgE concentrations (1,430-2,100 IU/ml).

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) also reported 7 patients from 5 families in Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina. These patients had mycobacterial and/or viral infections but no features of HIES. None had documented pyogenic or staphylococcal infections, fungal infections, or high serum IgE. P2 was the Turkish man born to first-cousin parents previously reported by Kilic et al. (2012). He had disseminated BCG lymphadenitis at 21 months of age, severe bacterial meningitis with CSF cultures positive for Brucella at 8 years, and shingles at 11 years. P3 was a Moroccan girl born to consanguineous parents. She was hospitalized at 13 years with suspected abdominal tuberculosis and developed ascites and a psoas abscess despite antimycobacterial treatment. She died of disseminated tuberculosis at 15 years. Her younger brother (P4) was hospitalized at 8 months for meningitis of unknown etiology. He had recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels; he was 15 years old and untreated at the time of the report. P5 was an Iranian boy born to consanguineous parents and vaccinated with BCG at birth. He developed right axillary lymphadenitis at 2 months and multiple cervical lymphadenitis at 4 months. At 4.5 years he developed paravertebral and psoas abscesses with fistulization and pulmonary involvement. His 2-year-old sister (P6) developed BCG lymphadenopathy lasting 1 month after vaccination at birth. At 1 year she was hospitalized for 1 week for an unknown viral infection of the skin. P7 was a 9-year-old Iranian girl born to consanguineous parents. She had pneumonia at 8 months. At 9 years she presented with fever and productive cough, and imaging showed diffuse bilateral micronodular lung infiltrations, hilar and mediastinal adenopathies, and cavitary consolidation in the right upper lobe, consistent with miliary tuberculosis. P8 was an Argentinian boy. He had herpes gingivostomatitis at 18 months of age, then aseptic meningitis and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions at 24 months, as well as exanthema subitum. He also had mild mental disability; it was not clearly established whether this was congenital or followed the meningitis. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infections.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy, aged 1 year and 11 months, who was the second child of young, nonconsanguineous parents. He was vaccinated with BCG on the third day after birth. He developed BCG disease with abscess and ulceration at the injection site and BCG-associated axillary lymph node tuberculosis. He also had recurrent respiratory tract infections, bacterial pneumonia, diarrhea, Salmonella infection, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, and was positive for influenza A and B IgM antibodies. Other features were delayed speech and a small head circumference. Serum IgG, IgA, IgE, and IgM were normal. The percentage of CD19+ B cells was increased and NK cells were decreased, without lymphopenia. He had no atopy, staphylococcal infection, or fungal infection. Wu et al. (2020) also reviewed 12 reported TYK2-deficient patients, including their own. Seven (58%) had intracellular bacterial infections, 7 (58%) had recurrent viral infections, 2 (17%) had rash or atopic dermatitis/eczema, and 3 (25%) had markedly increased serum IgE. None of the 12 had the facial features, abnormal bone development, pathologic fractures, delayed loss of deciduous teeth, or aneurysms seen in STAT3-related HIES.

paragraphs.text: In a Chinese boy with TYK2 deficiency born to nonconsanguineous parents, Wu et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.2395G-A transition in exon 17 of the TYK2 gene, resulting in a gly799-to-arg (G799R) substitution. The boy had BCG disease, Salmonella infection, recurrent respiratory infections, and pneumonia, with normal serum IgE. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. TYK2 mRNA was reduced and TYK2 protein was undetectable in the patient's cells. In HEK293T cells, TYK2 constructs carrying the mutation showed reduced mRNA and protein expression compared with wildtype. The variant was present in the gnomAD database.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated children of consanguineous Turkish parents who were hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia, Zhang et al. (2022) identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the TYK2 gene (P216Rfs*14), previously shown to be loss-of-expression. Family segregation analysis confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance. The pneumonia was moderate in a 2-year-old girl (P2) and critical in boys aged 4 (P3) and 9 (P4) years. The 3-year-old sister of P3 carried the same genotype and had a history of critical influenza pneumonia and disseminated varicella. ACE2-transduced fibroblasts from a homozygous patient failed to control SARS-CoV-2 replication and failed to induce ISGs in response to IFN-alpha-2b.
